explanations.explanation: This feature appears to detect contexts where the model substitutes a common subword ending (“‑er”) with a special, decorative delimiter character (rendered as “�”). In other words, it encodes a switch from a routine “‑er” continuation to a token representing a nonstandard typographic or formatting marker that often marks a stylistic or domain‐specific boundary.

It appears that the feature is sensitive to specific subword segments—affix‐ or morpheme‐like chunks embedded in proper names or culturally marked words—that signal a nonstandard (often foreign or regionally specific) linguistic identity.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on the final syllables of vivid, evaluative adjectives—morpheme chunks (like “‐ling,” “‐ating,” “‐or”) that signal heightened, sensory, or hyperbolic descriptions. In essence, the feature is capturing the stylistic and affective embellishment used to intensify descriptions.

It appears this feature “lights up” on the little function‐words—and especially the parts of phrases that set up comparisons or quantity limits. In contexts discussing numbers or exclusive items (e.g. “no fewer than …”, “only …”, “of …”, or contracted forms like “what’s”), the feature “knows” that a specific grammatical, quantitative/comparative element belongs there. Removing it causes the model to fall back to nonsensical letter strings (like “b” or “ell”) instead of the expected function word. So, abstractly, the feature appears to represent the network’s internal handle for marking and generating limitative or comparative constructions in numerical/quantitative contexts.

It appears the feature is detecting a punctuation–period token that marks a boundary (often after an abbreviation or proper name) and thereby signals a segmentation break in the text. In other words, it identifies when a period is functioning as an end‐marker (for a title, sentence, or heading), which in turn steers the model’s next‐token prediction.

This feature detects and signals when a period is used in abbreviated or acronymic contexts (such as titles, names, or product codes), helping the model distinguish abbreviation boundaries from full sentence endings.

It appears that this feature is detecting hyphenation boundaries—in other words, it signals when a hyphen (or similar punctuation) is splitting a word (or linking subword units) so that the model correctly segments and predicts the continuation of a compound expression.

It is a detector for subword‐boundary fragments—that is, a feature that lights up when a token is a split or inflectional piece of a compound or specially formatted word (e.g. hyphenated, slashed, or numeric/letter combinations) that needs to be reassembled into a full lexical unit.
This feature detects and processes the compound age adjective construction (e.g., “70‐year‐old”), cueing the formation of a hyphenated modifier that describes a person’s age.

It appears that the feature “lights up” on words that mark a unique or total quantification (or its negation)—for example, singular and negative indefinites like “one,” “every,” “nothing,” “no one” and related forms—which in turn primes the model to choose a syntactically and semantically appropriate continuation (e.g. favoring a copula “is” or other agreement over a generic article “a”).
